OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify anatomic, biomechanical, and pathophysiologic factors related to calcaneal stress
fractures.
Perform appropriate clinical work up of a patient in whom a calcaneal stress fracture is
suspected.
Formulate an appropriate nonsurgical treatment plan for a patient with a calcaneal stress
fracture.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Calcaneal stress fractures result from repetitive submaximal loading and/or decreased bone
density.
They most commonly involve the calcaneal tuberosity.

Pes cavus and hindfoot varus result in a less supple foot at heel strike and may predispose the
patient to stress fractures.
Factors related to a patient’s bone health and activity profile may play a role in
pathophysiology and must be considered as part of the diagnostic workup.
Epidemiology
Incidence of stress fractures ranges from 1% to 7% in the general athletic population.1,2
The incidence may be as high as 15% in runners.3
Among military recruits, the incidence has been estimated to be 2.6 per 10,000 person-years.4
The lower extremity is the location of 80% to 90% of stress fractures.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The calcaneus is the largest tarsal bone.
It must withstand compressive and tensile forces.
Heel strike while running produces loads 1.5 to 3.0 times body weight on the tuberosity.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
In the sagittal plane, the calcaneus typically has four discernable trabecular patterns:
one vertical, one longitudinal, and two obliquely oriented. Using finite element analysis,
Gefen and Seliktar6 determined that the vertical and posterior-oblique trabecular groups
support compressive forces, whereas the longitudinal and anterior oblique groups bear
tension (Figure 1).
Studies of heel strike versus midfoot strike running have demonstrated heel strike
running produces impact forces on the calcaneus tuberosity ranging from 1.5 to 3.0
times body weight.7

Etiology and Healing
Calcaneal stress fracture results from repetitive submaximal loading of bone, leading to the
accumulation of microfractures.
Such injury occurs across a spectrum from stress response to displaced fracture.1,8
Healing is via endochondral bone formation.9
Risk Factors
Female sex
Military recruits
High-level or escalating athletic activity
Tarsal coalition
Pes cavus deformity
Low bone mineral density

Impaired bone metabolism

Risk Factors
Calcaneal stress fractures are associated with certain demographic, behavioral, and
anatomic factors. Such factors can be categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic.10 Intrinsic
refers to host characteristics, and extrinsic refers to environmental and behavioral
characteristics.
Multiple factors may be at play in an individual patient. For example, the female athlete
triad was described in the 1990s as a syndrome of disordered eating, menstrual cycle
perturbation, and low bone density.11 Since then, the analogous male athlete triad has
been recognized as a syndrome of low energy availability, low bone mineral density, and
hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.12
Multifactorial risk also has been identified among military recruits. Niva et al13 reported
considerably increased risk among female military recruits and those entering training
with lower aerobic fitness.
Calcaneal stress fractures also are associated with altered foot mechanics. For example,
an association with pes cavus (Figure 2) and tarsal coalitions (Figure 3) has been
described.14 In these settings, normal foot biomechanics are altered, leading to stress
concentration in the heel and metatarsals.
Various causes of low bone mineral density and altered bone metabolism have been
reported in combination with calcaneal stress fracture. Examples include rheumatoid
arthritis15 and long-term use of chemotherapeutics.16

Classification
Calcaneal stress fractures are considered low-risk injuries.

Classification
Stress fractures generally are classified as low-risk or high-risk for progressing to
completion, displacement, delayed union, or nonunion.1,8 Low-risk stress fractures
include calcaneal stress fractures and fractures of the second and third metatarsal
bases, posteromedial tibia, and cuboid. High-risk fractures include those of the fifth
metatarsal base, second metatarsal base, navicular, and tibial shaft.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Calcaneal stress fractures typically occur insidiously in at-risk patients.

Patient History
A calcaneal stress fracture may occur insidiously. Initially, the pain may be constant. It
typically intensifies with activity and improves with rest, NSAIDs, and ice. A thorough
patient history and review of systems should be undertaken to identify intrinsic and
extrinsic risk factors, symptoms of metabolic disease, and exposure to medications
detrimental to bone health.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001013
6/16

Acute heel swelling, warmth, and bruising may occur with onset of the lesion.
Diffuse swelling may be present in subacute cases.
The foot should be examined to identify the point of maximal tenderness (Figure 4; Resource
1).
The calcaneal squeeze test is performed using medial and lateral compression of the
calcaneus on the weight-bearing heel. Lateral wall tenderness with palpation of the lateral
aspect of the tuberosity also is highly suggestive of a calcaneal stress fracture.
Figure 4 Clinical photograph of a foot shows the points of maximal tenderness in relation to the
most common causes of heel pain. The foot is shown with the toes to the right and the medial
aspect of the foot and ankle at the top. (Reproduced from Richardson DR, Richardson EG: Heel
pain, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1197-1203.)
Laboratory Studies
Vitamin D and calcium

Laboratory Studies

The treating physician should always consider assessing vitamin D and calcium levels,
especially in patients in northern latitudes.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Lateral and axial radiographs of the calcaneus should be obtained.
Comparisons should be made with contralateral or past ipsilateral radiographs.

Radiography
Initial radiographs may be unremarkable in appearance. Soft-tissue swelling may be
noted. A band of increased density may be visible in the posterior aspect of the
calcaneus 2 to 4 weeks after the onset of symptoms (Figure 5). A calcaneal stress
fracture usually is oriented vertically or obliquely in the tuberosity of the calcaneus.
Radiolucency from bony resorption can be observed 10 to 14 days after the onset of
symptoms. Radiodensity develops thereafter as a result of fracture healing.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can identify periosteal reaction, soft-tissue edema, and hypervascularity.

Ultrasonography
In a case series of calcaneal stress fractures identified via ultrasonography ordered to
evaluate soft-tissue injuries, Bianchi and Luong17 reported key findings such as
periosteal thickening with hypervascularity, cortical irregularity, and subcutaneous
edema. Among elite track athletes, ultrasonography is 81.4% as accurate compared with

MRI for the detection of bone stress injuries ranging from stress reaction to stress
fracture.18
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI depicts bone edema, periosteal reaction, and calcaneal stress reaction or fracture line.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred diagnostic imaging modality for evaluating stress injuries of bone.19
It allows for localization of the lesion, which may not be limited to the tuberosity, and it
may identify lesions in other bones.4
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scans may be positive if radiographs are negative.20
Computed Tomography
CT may be more helpful than MRI in evaluating the extent of bone healing.

Computed Tomography
In a study of the long-term clinical outcomes of navicular stress lesions (11 stress
fractures, 9 stress reactions), Burne et al21 reported that clinical measures did not
statistically align with cross-sectional imaging findings at final follow-up and suggested
that CT may characterize bone healing in this phase of recovery better than MRI (Figure
6).

overuse, and nerve entrapment conditions affecting the heel (Table 1).


Differential Diagnosis
Plantar fasciitis is the most likely alternative diagnosis. Bone bruising, entrapment of the
first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, fat pad atrophy, and tarsal tunnel syndrome also
should be considered. Heel pain in elderly patients and atypical presentation in any
patient should be investigated to rule out insufficiency fractures and tumors.
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:35 AM
AAOS | Calcaneal Stress Fracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001013
12/16

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management via off-loading and activity modifications usually is effective.
Initial management is restriction of painful activity for 4 to 6 weeks.
If the patient has pain with normal walking, a short leg cast or boot should be considered.
The patient is then allowed to return to activity gradually as the pain resolves.

Nonsurgical Management
In a study of published protocols, the mean time for orthosis use was 6 weeks.22
Patients with lower bone mineral density or impaired mineralization and a high-risk
fracture required longer periods of immobilization. The patient may need a referral to an
endocrinologist if metabolic abnormalities are suspected.
If a soft shoe or a cushioned insert is insufficient, heel off-loading may be helpful.
Compared with a neutral shoe, heel off-loading shoes or heel off-loading braces may
reduce heel plantar pressures by as much as 50%.23 In addition, a custom patellar
bearing brace can off-load the heel as the patient bears weight through the foot.24 This
brace can be modified via patten-bottom caliper suspension, which allows for
ambulation without bearing weight on the foot.25
Surgical Management
Calcaneal stress fractures do not require surgical management unless displacement occurs,
which is rare.
